name: Pogo Jumps
target: ankle stiffness, reactive strength, Achilles tendon loading
muscleText: Calves (gastrocnemius, soleus), Achilles tendon, plantar fascia
rationale: Pogo jumps develop the spring-like stiffness in the ankle and Achilles that makes running economy efficient. Short, rapid ground contacts train the stretch-shortening cycle at the ankle — the same mechanism used in every running stride.
evidence: Ankle stiffness improvements from pogo-style drills are well-supported in running economy research.

name: Ankling
target: ankle mechanics, foot strike pattern, cadence
muscleText: Tibialis anterior, calves (gastrocnemius, soleus), intrinsic foot muscles
rationale: Ankling drills reinforce the dorsiflexion-to-plantarflexion cycle that underlies efficient midfoot striking. Practising the pattern slowly and deliberately builds the neuromuscular blueprint before applying it at speed.
evidence: Common staple of elite running drill progressions; recommended in all major sprint and distance coaching frameworks.

name: A-Skips
target: hip drive, ground contact mechanics, coordination
rationale: A-skips teach the cyclical high-knee drive and quick ground contact that translates directly to faster cadence. The skip rhythm makes the drill accessible for any fitness level while still building hip flexor power.
evidence: Universal drill in track and field; used by elite distance runners for warm-up and technique reinforcement.

name: Jump Rope (Basic)
muscleText: Calves (gastrocnemius, soleus), Achilles tendon, core stabilisers
rationale: Jump rope is the single most time-efficient tool for building elastic ankle stiffness and rhythmic foot turnover. Even two minutes a day creates meaningful adaptation in the Achilles and calf complex.
evidence: Regularly prescribed in plyo progressions for runners due to its low-cost, high-frequency training effect on the stretch-shortening cycle.

name: Bounding
target: horizontal power, stride length, glute and hip extension
muscleText: Glutes (gluteus maximus), hamstrings, calves, hip flexors
rationale: Bounding exaggerates the push-off phase of the running stride, building the posterior-chain power that drives stride length. It bridges the gap between drills and true plyometric intensity.
evidence: Strong evidence that bounding improves running economy and maximal sprint velocity in distance runners.

name: Split-Squat Jumps
target: single-leg power, hip extension, deceleration control
rationale: Split-squat jumps load each leg independently, matching the unilateral demands of running and exposing asymmetries. The landing phase trains eccentric quad and glute strength critical for injury prevention.
evidence: Recommended for runners transitioning to single-leg plyometric loading.

name: Box Jumps
target: explosive leg power, reactive landing mechanics
rationale: Box jumps develop maximal concentric leg power and teach safe landing mechanics at moderate impact loads. Stepping down (rather than jumping off) limits eccentric stress, making this the appropriate Tier 2 entry for box work.
evidence: Well-established in athletic development for improving vertical force production translatable to uphill running and acceleration.

name: Broad Jumps
target: horizontal power, two-leg takeoff, landing control
rationale: Broad jumps maximise horizontal distance from a two-footed takeoff, directly training the forward propulsion mechanics of running. They build posterior-chain power and prepare the athlete for single-leg horizontal loading in Tier 3.
evidence: Broad jump performance correlates with sprint speed and is a common field test of horizontal power in runners.

name: Depth Jumps
target: maximal reactive strength, rapid force production, Achilles stiffness
muscleText: Calves (gastrocnemius, soleus), Achilles tendon, quadriceps, glutes
rationale: Depth jumps subject the body to the highest rates of stretch-shortening cycle loading available in training, building the reactive strength required for fast racing. They must only be used once an athlete has a solid Tier 2 base and sound landing mechanics.
evidence: Considered the gold-standard plyo stimulus for reactive strength index; requires a minimum strength base before prescription.

name: Single-Leg Reactive Hops
target: single-leg stiffness, ankle and Achilles loading, lateral stability
muscleText: Calves (gastrocnemius, soleus), Achilles tendon, tibialis anterior, intrinsic foot muscles, glute medius
rationale: Single-leg reactive hops replicate the exact loading pattern of distance running on one leg, making them the most specific plyo drill in the programme. They expose ankle and knee instability that bilateral exercises mask.
evidence: Closely mimics ground reaction force patterns of distance running; used in return-to-sport protocols post Achilles and ankle injury.

name: Drop Jumps
target: maximal reactive strength, contact time minimisation
muscleText: Calves (gastrocnemius, soleus), Achilles tendon, quadriceps, hamstrings
rationale: Drop jumps train the athlete to minimise ground contact time under high eccentric loading — the key adaption for sub-elite and elite racing pace. The focus is stiffness and speed of rebound, not height.
evidence: Used in elite sprint and distance programmes; one of the highest-load plyometric stimuli available.

name: Hurdle Series (Continuous)
target: continuous reactive strength, hip mobility under load, coordination at speed
muscleText: Calves, Achilles tendon, glutes, hip flexors (iliopsoas), hamstrings
rationale: Continuous hurdle hops combine rapid ground contact with full hip extension, training the same muscular coordination demanded in fast-finish racing scenarios. The series format accumulates fatigue to simulate late-race conditions.
evidence: Standard in elite sprint and middle-distance training for developing reactive leg stiffness and rhythm under accumulated fatigue.
